title_original: The lowdown on the Oscars international feature race
excerpt_original: A record 104 films are competing for the international feature Academy Award, including several by virtue of festival wins.

blocks.alt: La Bola Negra, Strawberries, The Meltdown, All Of A Sudden

blocks.text: Source: Carla Oset / Netflix / Cannes / Cinefrance Studios
La Bola Negra, Strawberries, The Meltdown, All Of A Sudden

It should come as no surprise that Screen International takes a particular interest in the international feature Oscar and its equivalent category at the Ba­fta Film Awards — we are headquartered in London, one of the world’s most globally attuned cities, have correspondents scattered all over the world, and our well-travelled critics and reporters assiduously cover the global festival beat.

This year, Ampas provided an alternative pathway to compete for the international feature Oscar: in addition to submission by country, winners of prizes at a number of A-list festivals became eligible. In the event, several of those festival winners — such as Venice Golden Lion recipient Woman Unknown — were selected by their home country in any case, but the shake-up is overdue and welcome. At Ba­fta, the majority of titles competing for the film not in the English language award are ones not eligible for the international feature Oscar.
Our guides covering all entries to these awards, at Oscar and Ba­fta, are below.

blocks.text: The growing international make-up of the voting academies goes hand in hand with increasing confidence and ambition from companies such as Neon and Netflix to break out of categories ringfenced for films not in the English language, and compete across the awards waterfront. Last year Joachim Trier’s Sentimental Value achieved nine Oscar nominations and eight at Ba­fta. The year before, Jacques Audiard’s Emilia Pérez accrued 13 Oscar and 11 Ba­fta nods (and four wins combined).

This time around, Spain’s Oscar entry La Bola Negra looks likely to lead the charge for non-English-language films — with other titles in hot pursuit. Look for wide engagement of voters across multiple categories for films that were chosen by countries for the Oscar (such as Possible Love ), and also ones that were not — the latter including Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster, Marine Atlan’s La Gradiva and Takashi Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus One .

Also in the mix is the Hebrew-language NAZA , from Israel’s Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, although it’s perhaps the documentary feature category at Ba­fta and Oscar where that film will have its strongest shot. The global box office suggests NAZA has already engaged a wide audience, the primary goal of a film seeking, most of all, to move hearts and minds.

Read Screen’s November 27 issue for more on the international awards race, and listen to our latest podcast , which features Ampas’ Meredith Shea on the decision to make festival winners eligible for the Oscar.
